strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem: the paper targets physically-plausible refraction/reflection of transparent objects in generative image models, an important and underexplored failure mode of current text-to-image systems.

Technically interesting approach: it enforces Snell's-law ray-traced pixel-to-pixel warping inside the diffusion trajectory and, crucially, synchronizes a perspective view with a concurrently generated 360-degree panorama to constrain refracted/reflected pixels that would otherwise be hallucinated. The Fresnel-based combination of refraction and reflection is a principled touch.
The method is training-free and integrates cleanly with an existing flow-matching backbone (Flux), making it relatively easy to adopt.

Qualitative results are convincing: the characteristic left-right/up-down flips and radial distortion of the background inside the glass sphere match the Blender references and clearly outperform both Flux inpainting and standard Flux, which is a strong signal that the physics is being respected.

Good supporting analyses: ablations on detail-preserving averaging, Laplacian pyramid warping, and time travel (Fig. 5, Tab. 3), plus sensitivity studies on refractive index and time-travel repeat counts in the supplement.
Reproducibility is reasonable: full prompts, hyperparameters, timestep/guidance settings, and an honest discussion of the limitations of the metrics are provided.
weaknesses: Evaluation is very narrow: only six indoor scene prompts, essentially all with a glass sphere, and a single baseline family (Flux inpainting / standard Flux). There is no comparison against closely related transparent-object/reflection methods (e.g., SynMirror, DiffusionLight) or other physics-guided generative approaches.

The quantitative evidence does not actually measure the central claim of optical accuracy. The authors themselves concede the Blender pseudo-ground-truth has incorrect lighting/color and missing data, so masked PSNR/LPIPS against it are unreliable, while CLIP and ImageReward measure prompt alignment rather than physical plausibility. No human study or dedicated physical-plausibility metric is provided.

The method rests on strong simplifying assumptions: a single transparent object, uniform refractive index, non-scattering material, access to an accurate 3D mesh and known pose, and reliable monocular depth. Object placement is heuristic (nearest horizontal surface near the optical axis), and object pose/scale are not controllable or optimized, limiting generality and robustness.

The claim that occluded/out-of-frame appearance is 'recovered' is overstated: it is synthesized by a generated panorama and then blended, i.e., hallucinated content constrained to be view-consistent, not recovered. Physical realism is also partly propped up by a separate black-box relighting/harmonization model for shadows and caustics.
Dependence on an external LLM (ChatGPT) for prompt decomposition and refractive-index extraction is brittle, with no analysis of failure modes or sensitivity to extraction errors.

The scope demonstrated is limited to a small set of simple, mostly spherical geometries; the supplement's more complex objects are still qualitative and use clean watertight meshes from RefRef, leaving the robustness of the pipeline under realistic mesh/depth noise unclear.

strengths: Introduces a novel and technically well-motivated approach for physically accurate refraction and reflection in generative image synthesis, enforcing Snell's law through pixel warping and synchronization rather than relying on hallucination.

The training-free method is clearly described and integrates naturally with flow-matching generative models, using cross-view synchronization with a generated panorama to plausibly fill occluded or out-of-frame refracted/reflected surfaces.

Provides strong qualitative evidence: the method correctly reproduces left-right/up-down flips, radial distortions, and scene-consistent refractions where Flux inpainting and standard Flux fail or produce implausible physics.

Quantitative results show substantial gains on masked PSNR (17.10 vs 11.24/11.18) and masked LPIPS (0.28 vs 0.51), with competitive or better CLIP and ImageReward scores, supporting the claim of improved physical fidelity.

The supplement is thorough: additional transparent object types (dog, cylinder, fox, sculpture, pyramid), refractive index sweeps, time-travel analysis, full prompts, and implementation details, which together improve reproducibility and demonstrate robustness beyond the glass sphere.

The method is well positioned relative to related work on relighting, reflections, and synchronized generation, and the problem is clearly framed as an important limitation of current text-to-image models.
weaknesses: Evaluation breadth is limited: the main paper focuses on six indoor scenes with a glass sphere, and although the supplement adds object types, all quantitative physical-fidelity comparisons rely on Blender-rendered pseudo-ground-truth rather than real captured images or a user study. Generalization to diverse real scenes, lighting, and materials remains untested.

The method relies on several restrictive assumptions: a single transparent object, uniform refractive index, non-scattering, no absorption, and access to an estimated 3D mesh, material, and pose. Object pose estimation is heuristic (horizontal surface near the optical axis), which limits applicability to more complex compositions.

The quantitative metrics are imperfect for measuring physical correctness. The Blender reference has incorrect lighting/colors and missing refracted data, the physical metrics are computed on masked grayscale images with histogram matching, and CLIP/ImageReward are not designed to assess refraction physics. ImageReward for the proposed method is also slightly below standard Flux.

The warping functions are precomputed from geometry estimated on the initial object-free image and are not updated during denoising; errors in depth estimation or 3D mesh generation may propagate as misalignments, and this sensitivity is not systematically analyzed.

Comparisons are limited to Flux inpainting and standard Flux generation. No comparison is made to other physics-aware or reflection-aware generative methods (e.g., SynMirror, DiffusionLight) or to classical rendering-based compositing baselines, which would better situate the contribution.
There are minor presentation issues, including an ambiguous Fresnel blending equation and dense notation in the light-transport section, which could be clarified for reproducibility.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: physically plausible generation of transparent refractive objects, where standard text-to-image models often fail.

Proposes a technically detailed, training-free pipeline that combines flow matching with ray-traced pixel correspondences based on Snell's law and Fresnel equations, plus cross-view synchronization with a generated panorama.

Includes an ablation study and qualitative comparisons showing that the proposed components (detail-preserving averaging, Laplacian pyramid warping, time travel) and physics-based warping can improve refraction plausibility over Flux inpainting and standard Flux generation.
The supplementary material extends results to several object geometries and refractive indices, suggesting the approach can handle more than a simple glass sphere in principle.
The paper is generally well organized, with clear figures and a readable description of the method.
weaknesses: Evaluation breadth is very limited: the main paper uses only 6 indoor scenes and a single glass sphere, with no real-world images, no human perceptual study, and no quantitative evaluation of complex objects in the main paper.

The quantitative evaluation is unreliable and partly circular: the Blender pseudo-ground truth is rendered from the same estimated geometry/appearance and is not lighting-harmonized; masked PSNR/LPIPS exclude exactly the unseen refracted regions where the proposed panorama synchronization matters; and CLIP/ImageReward measure prompt alignment rather than physical plausibility. The ablation in Table 3 even shows that removing time travel improves CLIP/ImageReward, undermining the claimed benefits.

The method relies on strong simplifying assumptions: a single non-scattering object, uniform refractive index, known 3D mesh/material/pose (or brittle LLM/TRELLIS extraction), and placement on a horizontal surface near the optical axis. This limits applicability to real transparent objects involving multiple objects, absorption, scattering, or non-uniform materials.

The pipeline depends on many external models (Flux, MoGe-2, TRELLIS, an LLM, and a relighting model) without systematic error-propagation analysis. Failures in any component could invalidate the generated result, and reproducibility is limited by these dependencies.

There are technical/presentation issues: Eq. 12 appears to contain duplicate c^R terms, making the Fresnel blending mathematically incorrect as written; there is no explicit limitations section; and no comparison is made to physically based rendering or other reflection/refraction-aware generative methods.

Novelty is incremental: the approach largely combines existing diffusion synchronization techniques with classical ray tracing, and the core contribution is an engineered pipeline rather than a fundamental advance. The claim of 'accurate refraction' is overstated given the restricted setting.

strengths: Addresses a clearly motivated and under-explored problem: generative models fail to render physically plausible refraction/reflection, and the paper provides a principled solution.

The method is technically sound and novel: it enforces Snell's Law and Fresnel equations via precomputed ray-traced pixel-to-pixel warping functions and synchronizes a perspective view with a panorama branch at every denoising step, all in a training-free manner on top of an existing flow-matching model.

The cross-view (perspective + panorama) synchronization is a clever and effective way to constrain pixels that are occluded or outside the camera frustum, directly targeting the core failure of baselines.

Quantitative results are strong and consistent on the physics-oriented metrics: masked PSNR 16.51 vs. 12.68 (best baseline) and masked LPIPS 0.24 vs. 0.48, and the method wins on every individual scene in Table 3.

Evaluation is reasonably broad: 300 scene-object combinations, multiple strong baselines (FLUX-dev, FLUX.2-dev, Qwen-Image, SD3.5, FLUX Inpainting), ablations of reflection modeling, panorama sync, relighting, DPA, LPW, and time travel, plus real-world image-pair examples.
The paper is honest about its limitations and about the reliability of the Blender pseudo-ground-truth, which strengthens credibility.
Qualitative comparisons (Figs. 3, 9, 10) clearly show baselines hallucinating implausible interiors while the proposed method produces the expected left-right/up-down flips and radial warping.
weaknesses: The setting is heavily constrained: a single transparent object, piecewise-constant uniform refractive index, non-scattering material, placed on a horizontal surface near the optical axis, with a known 3D mesh and refractive index. This limits generality relative to the broad framing of the paper.

The central 'optically accurate' claim is only approximate: the geometry used for ray tracing comes from an estimated depth map (MoGe-2) and a lifted 3D model, so the refraction is consistent with an estimated scene rather than the true scene.

The primary per-pixel evidence (masked PSNR/LPIPS) is measured against a Blender render built from the same estimated geometry, and the authors themselves acknowledge this pseudo-ground-truth has incorrect lighting and missing data where refracted surfaces are unobserved. This weakens the reliability of the headline quantitative claim.

CLIP and ImageReward scores do not favor the method (e.g., ImageReward 0.18 for FLUX.2 vs. -0.32 for the proposed method); the paper argues this is expected, but it means the method is not shown to improve overall prompt alignment or aesthetics.

The relighting post-processing, which is important for visual plausibility, measurably degrades the per-pixel metrics, indicating a tension between the reported numbers and the final presented outputs.
Inference is expensive (~126 s per perspective-panorama pair on an A100), which may limit practical adoption.
Several components rely on external heuristics (LLM-based refractive index extraction, SAM 3 surface segmentation, TRELLIS mesh generation), and their failure modes are not thoroughly analyzed.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely under-explored and well-motivated failure mode of modern generative models: transparent/refractive objects, where pixel colors inside the object are constrained by surfaces observed elsewhere in the image. The problem framing in Section 1 (refraction as an *indirectly* observed surface, unlike reflection which can be hallucinated) is crisp and correct.

The method is a novel, principled, and training-free combination of ideas: ray-traced pixel-to-pixel warp maps computed from Snell's law and the object/background geometry (Sec. 4.1), an auxiliary 360-degree panorama branch to fill occluded/out-of-frame pixels, per-denoising-step cross-view synchronization using Euler clean-latent estimates warped and blended in *pixel* space (Eqs. 9-11, 14), and Fresnel-based combination of refracted and reflected radiance (Eqs. 12-13). This goes meaningfully beyond prior synchronized-generation work (SyncDiffusion, SyncTweedies, SyncSDE, LookingGlass), which the related work section positions well.

The qualitative evidence in Figures 1 and 3 is compelling: baselines (FLUX inpainting with the exact object mask, FLUX-dev, FLUX.2, Qwen-Image, SD3.5) produce un-refracted or hallucinated content inside the object (e.g., sofa missing behind the sphere in the living room, TV/speakers absent in the karaoke scene, mountains not warped in the landscape scene), while the proposed method reproduces the expected left-right/up-down flips and radial warping visible in the Blender reference. Figure 9/10 extend this to cylinders, pyramids, and complex meshes (fox, dog, sculpture), where FLUX inpainting degrades notably.

Quantitatively, the gains in the physics-sensitive metrics are large and consistent: masked PSNR 16.51 vs 12.66 for FLUX inpainting and LPIPS 0.24 vs 0.47, with per-scene consistency across all ten scenes (Table 3), while CLIP/ImageReward are essentially preserved (no sacrifice of text alignment or aesthetics).

The ablation suite is thorough for a paper of this type: reflection modeling vs. panorama synchronization vs. relighting (Table 2, Fig. 6), detail-preserving averaging / Laplacian pyramid warping / time travel (Table 4, Fig. 13), time-travel repeat-count study (Fig. 12), and a refractive-index sweep showing sensitivity to material estimation (Fig. 11).

Reproducibility is reasonably good: the pipeline is built on public components (FLUX-dev, MoGe-2, TRELLIS, SAM 3, ChatGPT) with concrete hyperparameters (T=20 steps, guidance 3.5, lambda=0.5, 5 Laplacian levels, 3 time-travel repeats), full prompts in the supplement (Fig. 7), and runtime reported (~126 s per perspective-panorama pair on an A100).

The paper is honest about limitations (Sec. 6): absorption/tinting, multiple materials, birefringence, lighting/shadow handling via source estimation, and extension to video are explicitly flagged as future work rather than overclaimed.
weaknesses: The core evaluation rests on a pseudo-ground-truth that the authors themselves characterize as unreliable: the Blender render is not harmonized with respect to lighting, the reflected background is missing, and regions where refracted surfaces are not directly observed are absent. Masked PSNR with histogram matching further decouples the metric from true physical accuracy, and the absolute value (16.5 dB) indicates substantial residual deviation. Since the central claim is *perceptual/physical plausibility*, the absence of any human or perceptual study (e.g., forced-choice on refraction correctness) is a material gap in the evidence.

The setup requires a large amount of externally supplied, largely hand-specified information: an accurate object mesh (TRELLIS), an LLM-derived refractive index, an LLM-decomposed prompt (p, p-, p^360), an object-free reference image I_0-, a monocular depth map (MoGe-2), and a placement heuristic (object bottom-center on a horizontal surface near the optical axis, segmented by SAM 3). The paper assumes a single non-scattering object with uniform index, and provides no analysis of how errors in depth, segmentation, mesh quality, or index estimation propagate to the output. Sensitivity to depth/geometry error, in particular, is untested even though the whole warp-map construction depends on it.

No comparison is made against the most obvious non-generative alternative: directly rendering the placed mesh against the estimated environment/panorama with physically-based rendering and then harmonizing the result (i.e., essentially the Blender reference plus a relighting step). Without such a baseline, the paper does not isolate how much of the benefit comes from the diffusion synchronization versus simply from ray-traced warping/compositing, and does not justify why generation is needed at all rather than classical rendering plus harmonization.

Real-world validation is thin: only two image pairs (Fig. 5), both with a sphere, and in both cases I_0- is taken from a *paired photograph* rather than produced by the pipeline, which bypasses exactly the failure modes (generation of the object-free scene, depth estimation) that would matter in practice.

Consistency between the perspective view and the auxiliary panorama is only weakly enforced. The panorama is generated from a separate prompt p^360 and the two branches are related only through warping and blending; the paper assumes the two are 'compatible' but never analyzes cases where the panorama content disagrees with the perspective scene (different room layout, different objects), which would be a natural failure mode of the design.

Equation (12) as written reads c' = (1/2)(R_p + R_s)(c^R - c^R) + c^R, which collapses to c^R. Presumably the intended expression is (c^R - c^R) with reflection minus refraction, but as presented the derivation is either a typo or an error in how reflected and refracted contributions are weighted; this needs to be corrected/verified, and the sign/weighting convention made explicit.

Scope and generality remain narrow relative to the framing: one transparent object per image, resting on a horizontal surface near the optical axis, with fixed index and no absorption, scattering, or overlapping transparent objects. Several results still show residual mismatch (e.g., the pyramid/sculpture cases in Fig. 10), so 'optically-accurate' overstates what is demonstrated; 'optically-plausible and physically-constrained' would be more defensible.

Practical cost is not fully characterized: ~126 s per image on an A100 excludes preprocessing (depth, TRELLIS mesh generation, SAM 3, LLM queries, relighting), and the relighting post-process is applied 20 times with a PSNR-based selection. A total-cost breakdown and a discussion of when this is acceptable would strengthen the paper.

strengths: The paper targets a genuinely under-addressed and well-motivated failure mode of modern generative models: refraction. The framing in Fig. 1 and the introduction (refracted rays constrain pixels inside the object to agree with pixels observed elsewhere in the image) is correct, clearly stated, and useful as a problem statement.

The core technical idea is creative and grounded in optics: precomputing pixel-to-pixel warp fields by ray tracing through a 3D mesh with Snell's law (Eqs. 6-8), then enforcing them inside the flow-matching denoising trajectory, with a second 360-degree panorama branch to supply content for occluded/out-of-frame rays and Fresnel-based combination of refracted and reflected contributions (Eqs. 12-13). This is a sensible, non-obvious design that extends synchronized-generation ideas into a physics-constrained setting.

Qualitative evidence is strong and visually compelling. In Figs. 3, 9, and 10 the baselines (FLUX inpainting, FLUX-dev, FLUX.2-dev, Qwen-Image, SD3.5) plainly fail to produce the expected inverted/radially distorted background inside the sphere, while the proposed method does; the object-free image I0-, perspective image I0, and panorama I0^360 in Fig. 4 are mutually consistent.

The paper is reasonably self-critical in places: it acknowledges that relighting trades per-pixel metrics for realism (Table 2) and that the Blender pseudo-ground-truth has incorrect lighting and missing data, and it provides ablations over reflection modeling, panorama synchronization, detail-preserving averaging, Laplacian pyramid warping, and time travel.

The method is training-free on top of a released flow-matching model, and the supplementary material gives prompt templates, ray-tracing/Laplacian-warping details, and time-travel settings, which aids partial reproduction.
weaknesses: The headline quantitative result (masked PSNR 16.51 vs 12.68 for the best baseline; LPIPS 0.24 vs 0.47) is measured against a Blender pseudo-ground-truth that the authors themselves declare unreliable: the light sources/colors differ, the reflected background is absent, and regions where refracted surfaces are unobserved are missing. Table 2's caption states these metrics 'are not a fully reliable guide to performance,' yet they are the paper's central quantitative evidence. There is no alternative validation of refraction fidelity.

The evaluation is partly circular: the Blender reference is rendered from the same estimated depth/geometry (MoGe-2, Section 4) and the same object-free appearance I0- that the method itself consumes, so agreement with the reference partly reflects shared geometry rather than demonstrated physical correctness.

There is no human perceptual study, even though the paper's central claim is perceptual/physical plausibility. CLIP and ImageReward measure text alignment and aesthetics, not refraction correctness, and the paper reports that its method is worse than FLUX on ImageReward (-0.32 vs -0.20).

The comparison protocol gives the proposed method privileged information that the text-to-image baselines do not receive: Snellcaster is conditioned on the object-free image I0-, an explicit mask, a 3D mesh, a pose, and a refractive index, whereas FLUX-dev/FLUX.2/Qwen/SD3.5 generate from the prompt alone. This asymmetry is not discussed or controlled, and the 'same random seed' justification is not a substitute for matched conditioning.

The method relies on a long chain of fragile, unvalidated assumptions: an accurate mesh from TRELLIS, a correct refractive index queried from an LLM (the supplement notes it 'typically returns a value of 1.5'), accurate pose via a heuristic placement on a horizontal surface near the optical axis using SAM 3, accurate monocular depth, and a single non-scattering object with uniform IOR. No sensitivity or error-propagation analysis is given for mesh error, wrong IOR, non-horizontal placement, multiple objects, or transmissive/scattering materials, and the 300-item evaluation set is constructed to satisfy exactly these assumptions.
Evaluation breadth is narrow: 10 prompts x 5 variations, all single-object-on-a-horizontal-surface indoor/outdoor scenes. The 'real-world' evaluation (Fig. 5) is two image pairs and qualitative only.

Novelty is largely a recombination of existing components: Laplacian pyramid warping is taken from LookingGlass [3], per-step synchronization of multiple diffusion paths from SyncDiffusion/SyncTweedies/SyncSDE, plus standard Fresnel blending. The genuinely new deltas (applying Snell's-law warp fields inside the loop, and a panorama branch for occluded rays) are reasonable but incremental, and reflection is modeled only approximately (single reflection path; secondary reflections ignored; reflected content is effectively hallucinated through the panorama), which undercuts the 'optically accurate / physically accurate' framing.

Reporting inconsistencies make the ablation hard to interpret: the main table (with relighting, 16.51 PSNR) and the ablation table (without relighting, on a different six-scene subset, 18.21 PSNR) are not reconciled, and relighting is shown to degrade PSNR/LPIPS (17.10/0.28 vs 18.21/0.24) yet is included in the main results, so the reader cannot tell which configuration produces the reported numbers.

Practical cost and reproducibility: ~126 s per perspective/panorama pair on an A100 (preprocessing excluded), and the pipeline depends on several external systems (FLUX.1 Kontext API, MoGe-2, TRELLIS, SAM 3, ChatGPT for IOR extraction, a relighting model). No code release is indicated, and the pose/IOR heuristics make exact reproduction difficult.
